When Rare Encounters Define You: Zoe Williams Reflects on the Power of Infrequent Workplace Impressions

Overview

Zoe Williams, a columnist for The Guardian, uses a personal anecdote to illustrate how brief, twice‑a‑year professional encounters can leave lasting impressions that shape how colleagues perceive us. In her comment‑free piece published on 27 October 2026, Williams recounts arriving at a photo‑shoot drenched from a bike ride, clutching a handful of Haribo sweets, and becoming the subject of a series of well‑meaning but pointed remarks from the photographer and a client. The story serves as a springboard for a broader reflection on the social dynamics of limited‑frequency work relationships.

The anecdote in detail

On a rainy day that Williams describes as “the first rainy day in folk memory,” she arrived at a studio for a shoot with a photographer. She had cycled to the venue, tucked her trousers into her socks, and consequently arrived “soaking wet,” with water pooling around her ankles and soaking the rest of her body. The studio’s Labrador recoiled, prompting the photographer to recall their previous meeting in March:

> “You were really wet last time!”

Williams replied, “Well, it’s a wet country,” before a client interjected, “It’s actually in unprecedented drought, but fine.” The photographer then suggested she consider wet‑weather clothing for cycling, to which Williams quipped that this was the first time she had thought about it. A colleague added, “You ate all the Haribos last time,” a claim Williams neither confirms nor denies. The conversation continued with a light‑hearted suggestion to “have breakfast,” highlighting how quickly small details become talking points.

Social dynamics of infrequent professional contacts

Williams’ narrative underscores a well‑documented social‑psychology finding: first impressions, especially when formed from limited observation, can become disproportionately influential. Research shows that people often rely on salient, memorable details—such as being wet or eating candy—to construct a mental shortcut about a colleague’s character or habits. When interactions are rare, these shortcuts are rarely updated, leading to a static perception that may not reflect the person’s broader behavior.

The piece also touches on the role of humor and self‑deprecation in defusing potentially awkward moments. By acknowledging the photographer’s comment and the client’s joke, Williams demonstrates a coping strategy that can mitigate the negative impact of being typecast by a single incident.

Practical takeaways for readers

  • Mind the memorable moments: In settings where you see a colleague only a few times a year, be aware that any conspicuous incident (e.g., arriving wet, a wardrobe mishap) may stick in their memory.
  • Use humor strategically: Light‑hearted responses can turn a potentially judgmental comment into a shared joke, reducing the risk of lasting negative impressions.
  • Prepare for variability: If your role involves sporadic face‑to‑face meetings, consider practical preparations (e.g., weather‑appropriate attire) that pre‑empt obvious talking points.
  • Follow‑up when possible: A brief email or message after a meeting can subtly reshape the narrative, highlighting professionalism beyond the anecdotal detail.

Comparison with broader workplace trends

Williams’ experience mirrors a growing trend in modern work environments where remote collaboration and project‑based contracts limit in‑person contact. A 2024 Gallup survey found that 38 % of workers reported “limited personal interaction” with teammates, and 22 % felt that occasional meetings left them vulnerable to being judged on isolated incidents. While Williams’ story is anecdotal, it aligns with these broader patterns, suggesting that the phenomenon is not unique to her but part of a larger shift in professional socialization.

Upcoming Guardian event

The article concludes with a reminder of The Guardian’s Year in Review 2026, scheduled for Tuesday 1 December 2026. The event will feature Williams alongside John Crace, Pippa Crerar, Jonathan Liew, and Lucy Mangan, offering “candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises” about the year’s defining stories.
